messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Insurance Agent
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Prevention: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Robert was seven years old when his uncle came home smelling of cheap whiskey, the same smell that now stopped him mid-stride outside a liquor store. His uncle had been the one person his mother trusted to watch him while she worked nights, and for three years that trust was repaid with a palm that left bruises and a belt that left welts. No one ever asked about the marks. No one ever came. The man still lived two towns over, unpunished, unaccountable — a fact that had calcified into a bitter certainty: the people responsible had faced no consequences, and that meant the world was not a place where safety was enforced.

The smell of alcohol could still hijack his nervous system in an instant. It would waft from a passerby’s breath or from a bar as he walked past, and suddenly he was not a seventy-one-year-old insurance agent on a sidewalk — he was a child again, waiting for the footsteps. The memory came as a fragment, just a flash of a brown leather belt and a hand, more vivid and real than his actual surroundings. He could smell it — the whiskey, the stale sweat — as if the air had changed. That olfactory recall did not stay contained; it triggered the old appraisal that his body was a traitor, still reacting as if danger were present when logic told him he was safe. And because the abuser had never faced justice, he had come to believe that strangers, too, were unaccountable — that any ordinary approach could turn into a violation.

Working as an insurance agent required talking to strangers daily. Every new client on the phone or at the desk felt like a potential threat. A friendly hello from a neighbor on his porch could send his heart racing. He would then check his locks twice, sometimes three times, listening for the sound of footsteps on his stairs or the click of a key in the lock — an intrusion monitoring that had become second nature. These false alarms, reacting as if he were in danger when nothing was wrong, only deepened the appraisal that his own body was an enemy, that he could not trust its signals. The stranger trigger and the threat of intrusion fed each other: a stranger’s approach activated the threat system; the threat system, in turn, made him see strangers as more dangerous than they were.

To keep the memories at bay, Robert had developed quiet rituals. Before answering the door, he would count to seven under his breath — seven for the years of abuse — and believe that if he did it perfectly, nothing bad would happen that day. He kept his mind occupied constantly, filling his hours with paperwork, radio, crossword puzzles, anything to avoid the sudden fragments that could surface without warning. He stopped watching television dramas or reading news stories that involved child abuse; he knew the triggers were too close. But these strategies also reinforced the sense that something required constant vigilance. The mental rituals implied that danger was always latent, that without them he would be vulnerable, and that his own mind could not be trusted to simply let the past lie. Each ritual confirmed the betrayal narrative: no one had protected him then, so he had to protect himself now, even from his own thoughts.

The memories themselves were sporadic but punishing. A fragment would appear — the feel of a hand on his collar, the sound of a belt buckle — and vanish just as quickly, leaving him disoriented. Those fragments often brought the smell with them, and the smell was the most direct link to the original threat. Because the memories felt more real than his ordinary life, they overrode his present-moment safety cues, triggering the same defensive reactions he had as a child. He would freeze, scan the room, listen for footsteps. The memory fed the threat; the threat, in turn, made the memory more intrusive — a loop that tightened with each pass.

Now, at seventy-one, Robert had begun to notice that his avoidance was costing him. A colleague had retired, and he was forced to take on more client-facing work. He dreaded each call. He had considered early retirement but worried that he could not afford it and that the empty hours would leave him alone with the fragments. His sleep had grown restless; he often woke at 2 a.m., sure he had heard someone in the apartment. Last week a siren from an ambulance passing his building sent him to the floor without thinking. That was the moment he finally called the clinic. He was tired of counting, tired of checking locks, tired of being afraid of a man who was old and might not even be alive. What frightened him most was the possibility that the fear would never stop — that his body would always be the enemy, and that the world he had to live in would always feel as dangerous as the one he had survived.
